notes.summary: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the individual words. Break the ice has nothing to do with ice; it means to start a conversation. SSC asks for the meaning of an idiom, often inside a sentence.

concepts.title: Do not read literally
concepts.body: The literal meaning is almost always a trap option. Ask: what does this phrase suggest about a person or situation?

concepts.title: Use the sentence
concepts.body: If the idiom is in a sentence, the situation tells you whether the meaning is positive or negative. After the failure, he was down in the dumps → negative feeling → sad.

concepts.title: Learn in groups
concepts.body:
Group idioms by theme to remember them:
  • Difficulty: in hot water, in a fix, between the devil and the deep sea
  • Ease: a piece of cake, plain sailing
  • Secrecy: let the cat out of the bag, spill the beans

varieties.name: Meaning of the idiom
varieties.how: Recall the figurative meaning; eliminate the literal option.

steps: It means working or studying late into the night.
example.answer: To work late into the night

varieties.name: Idiom in a sentence
varieties.how: Read the context for tone, then pick the matching figurative meaning.

example.q: The new manager turned over a new leaf after the warning.
steps: A warning suggests he changed his behaviour.
Turn over a new leaf = start behaving better.

tips: Revise 10 idioms a day with flashcards; meanings rarely change.
If unsure, decide the tone (positive/negative) and remove options with the wrong tone.
traps: The literal option (e.g. 'to actually spill beans') is placed to catch guessers.
Similar idioms with different meanings: at sea (confused) vs all at sea (completely confused) vs a drop in the ocean (tiny amount).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A piece of cake
questions.solution: A piece of cake means a task that is very easy to do.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bold idiom.
Nobody knew about the surprise party until Rahul let the cat out of the bag.
questions.solution: Let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret by mistake. The context (surprise party) confirms it.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To hit the nail on the head
options: To say exactly the right thing
questions.solution: Hit the nail on the head = describe exactly what is causing a situation; to be precisely correct.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bold idiom.
With exams next week, Priya is burning the candle at both ends.
options: Exhausting herself by working too much
questions.solution: Burn the candle at both ends = overwork by staying up late and getting up early, wearing oneself out.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A red herring
questions.solution: A red herring is a clue or issue that draws attention away from the real question.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the bold idiom.
The opposition's promises turned out to be a flash in the pan; nothing came of them.
options: A sudden success that does not last
questions.solution: A flash in the pan = something that looks impressive at first but quickly fails or fades. nothing came of them confirms it.
